Family Health

Genital sores and vulval ulcers: causes, testing and care

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A new genital sore can be worrying, but its appearance alone rarely gives a reliable answer. Infections, irritation and inflammatory conditions can look similar, so an assessment is more useful than trying to diagnose it from a photograph.

Sores, blisters and lumps are not all the same thing

The vulva is the external genital area around the vaginal opening, including the labia. The vagina is the internal canal. A lesion may occur on the vulva, near the anus or inside the vagina. Noticing where it is can help describe the problem, but a photograph or a mirror check cannot reliably identify the cause.

An ulcer is an open break in the skin or mucosal surface. A blister contains fluid, while a wart, an inflamed hair follicle or a cyst may appear as a raised bump without being an ulcer. A lesion can change as it heals, breaks open or becomes irritated. Some are painful or itchy; others cause little discomfort. A painless sore still needs attention.

What symptoms should you mention?

Tell the clinician when the area changed, whether there is one lesion or several, and whether it is growing, crusting, bleeding or releasing fluid. Burning, itching, pain with sex, pain when urinating, pelvic pain and changes in vaginal discharge can help guide assessment. A bad smell is not required for infection, and normal-looking discharge does not exclude one.

Also mention fever, swollen glands, a recent illness, mouth ulcers, a rash elsewhere, new medicines and any episodes like this before. Some infections and inflammatory conditions affect more than one body area. Recent shaving, friction, a new detergent or an intimate-care product can also be relevant. These details help avoid assuming that every genital symptom has the same cause.

Herpes, syphilis and other infections that cause ulcers

Genital herpes and syphilis are important causes of genital ulcers in sexually active adults. Their frequency varies by location and population, and more than one infection can be present. Herpes may begin with tingling or blisters that become painful sores, but many people do not show this textbook pattern.

A primary syphilis sore is often painless and may be hidden inside the vagina or anus. However, sores can be painful, multiple or unusual. A sore disappearing does not mean syphilis has been cured. Blood testing, treatment and follow-up remain important because untreated infection can later damage other parts of the body.

Chancroid is a bacterial cause of painful ulcers in some regions; other less common infections may be considered according to travel and exposure. Oral, vaginal or anal sex and shared sex toys can transmit some infections. Herpes can also spread from an oral cold sore during oral sex, or from skin carrying the virus without a visible sore. A first noticed outbreak does not establish when infection happened or who transmitted it.

Warts and molluscum usually form bumps rather than open sores

Genital warts are linked to certain types of human papillomavirus, or HPV. They may be individual growths or clusters and can sometimes itch, bleed or become irritated. They are not usually open ulcers. A clinician should check a lesion that looks like a wart but is bleeding, changing or not behaving as expected.

Molluscum contagiosum is a viral skin infection that typically produces small raised spots with a central dimple. It spreads through skin contact and can occur without sexual contact, especially in children. In adults, genital spots may follow sexual contact. Scratching or picking can inflame the spots and damage the skin.

Do not use ordinary hand or foot wart-removal acids on genital skin, and do not squeeze a bump to see what comes out. Treatments differ: some lesions can be observed, while others need a prescribed cream or a procedure. A label such as wart, cyst or ulcer should follow assessment rather than a guess.

Nonsexual causes deserve the same careful attention

Eczema and contact dermatitis can make the vulva itchy, inflamed or cracked. Irritation from soaps, fragrances, wipes, detergents or friction can contribute; not all eczema is an allergy. Vulvovaginitis means inflammation of the vulva and vagina and is a description, not a single diagnosis. Scratching can create breaks in the skin that may become infected.

Ingrown hairs and inflamed follicles often affect hair-bearing skin after shaving or friction. A cyst is a contained lump, and a Bartholin cyst occurs near one side of the vaginal opening. A cyst that becomes infected may form a painful abscess. These problems are distinct from a primary ulcer and cannot all be prevented simply by washing more.

Aphthous ulcers can develop after an illness, including in someone who has never had sexual contact. This pattern is particularly relevant in children and adolescents. Other possibilities include inflammatory skin disease, Behçet’s disease, Crohn’s disease, trauma or a reaction to a medicine. The history and examination determine which tests or specialist referrals are useful. A genital ulcer alone is not evidence of sexual activity.

Persistent sores or bleeding need assessment

A sore that does not heal, a growing lump, persistent itching, a new thickened or discoloured patch, or bleeding unrelated to a period should be examined. Most such symptoms have causes other than cancer, but a persistent lesion can occasionally be a sign of vulval cancer or a precancerous change.

Do not keep treating the same area with over-the-counter creams while it continues to change. A clinician may recommend a small biopsy if the diagnosis is uncertain or treatment is not helping. A routine cervical-screening appointment is not a substitute for assessing a visible vulval lesion.

What happens at the appointment?

A primary-care clinician, gynaecologist or sexual-health service can assess the area. They may ask about symptoms, skin conditions, medicines, pregnancy and sexual exposure. These questions guide care; they are not a judgement. Ask for a chaperone or support person if you want one, and ask the examiner to explain each step and pause if needed.

A fresh sore may be swabbed for herpes or other organisms. Blood tests commonly include syphilis testing, and HIV testing is offered as part of genital-ulcer assessment if status is not already known. Other STI tests may be appropriate. Not everyone needs the same panel, and timing matters: a negative test early after exposure may need follow-up.

A healed lesion can be harder to test, so do not delay an appointment just to see whether it disappears. Some ulcers remain unexplained after initial tests and need review. If a first herpes episode or infectious syphilis is strongly suspected, a clinician may start treatment before results return because early treatment matters.

Gentle care while waiting to be seen

Rinse the external area gently with lukewarm water and pat dry. A short sitz bath, with the hips and affected area in comfortable warm water, may soothe pain. Avoid hot water, scrubbing, antiseptics, fragranced washes and vaginal douching. Plain water is a reasonable starting point; salt or bicarbonate mixtures are not necessary for every unexplained lesion and can sting.

Wear loose, comfortable clothing and avoid shaving over sore or swollen skin. Do not pick, pop or squeeze lesions. A wrapped cool compress may ease discomfort; do not place ice directly on the skin. Ask a pharmacist about a suitable pain reliever and a clinician about any barrier ointment or topical pain treatment.

Passing urine while gently pouring lukewarm water over the external area can reduce stinging. If pain prevents you from urinating, seek urgent care rather than trying to manage it only with baths. Avoid sexual contact involving the affected area until the cause has been assessed and you have advice about when it is safe to resume.

Treatment depends on the cause

Antibiotics treat selected bacterial infections, including syphilis and chancroid, but not herpes or every irritated lump. Herpes antivirals can shorten or lessen episodes and, for some people, suppress recurrences. They do not remove the virus from the body. A first episode should be assessed promptly even if it has already lasted several days.

Inflammatory skin conditions may need a prescribed corticosteroid or other targeted treatment. A steroid such as hydrocortisone is not a universal cream for an undiagnosed genital sore. Antifungal, anti-itch and pain treatments likewise depend on the diagnosis and the location; unnecessary products can irritate or delay appropriate care.

Some small uncomplicated cysts need no procedure, while a painful abscess may need drainage and sometimes antibiotics. Wart treatments and persistent skin-disease plans are different again. Complete the prescribed course and attend follow-up rather than stopping because the surface looks better. Ask what improvement to expect and when a lack of improvement should trigger reassessment.

Reducing transmission and future irritation

Condoms and other barriers reduce many STI risks, but herpes, HPV and syphilis can involve skin outside the area covered. Avoid oral, vaginal and anal sex during active herpes symptoms, including the tingling that may precede sores, until the lesions have healed. For another diagnosed infection, follow the clinic’s specific advice about treatment completion and resuming sex.

Discuss testing and treatment with partners when an STI is diagnosed. Their needs depend on the infection: they should not automatically take the same medicine or assume that no symptoms means no infection. A sexual-health clinic can help with confidential partner notification and prevention advice. Clean shared sex toys as recommended and use a new barrier between users or body sites.

For irritation-related problems, identify products or activities that worsen symptoms and avoid them. Gentle care is more helpful than aggressive cleaning. Pause shaving when skin is inflamed, and seek advice for repeated ingrown hairs or cysts. Not every recurrence can be prevented, and recurring disease is not a sign of poor hygiene.

When to seek urgent help and what recovery may involve

Arrange prompt assessment for a new genital ulcer, blisters, unexplained bleeding or a changing lesion. Seek same-day urgent care for severe pain, inability to urinate, fever with a rapidly enlarging tender lump, spreading inflammation or feeling very unwell. Severe pelvic pain, collapse or rapid deterioration requires emergency care.

If you are pregnant and develop new genital sores or think you have been exposed to syphilis or herpes, contact your maternity or sexual-health team promptly. The timing of infection matters for pregnancy and birth planning, especially a first herpes episode later in pregnancy. A child or adolescent with painful ulcers also needs appropriate clinical assessment rather than assumptions about the cause.

Recovery depends on the diagnosis. Some infections can be cured; herpes and chronic inflammatory skin conditions may need a plan for recurrences. Untreated chlamydia or gonorrhoea can contribute to PID, tubal scarring, infertility and ectopic pregnancy, but those are not universal consequences of herpes, warts or every genital sore. Syphilis has its own systemic and pregnancy complications. Getting the correct diagnosis helps address the actual risks and avoid unnecessary fear.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Genital ulcers need assessment because appearance and pain patterns overlap. Testing may include herpes, syphilis and HIV as appropriate.

Nonsexual causes are important, especially in children and adolescents; treatment and long-term risks depend on the actual diagnosis.

How BeMama can help

Describe what changed and seek care without embarrassment. You can ask for explanations, a chaperone and a clear follow-up plan.

When to seek help

Seek urgent care for inability to urinate, severe pain, fever with worsening swelling or feeling very unwell. New genital sores in pregnancy need prompt maternity or sexual-health advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A wart, cyst, blister and open ulcer are different types of lesion.
  • Herpes and syphilis matter, but not every sore is sexually transmitted.
  • A painless or healed sore can still need testing.
  • Avoid squeezing lesions or applying random genital creams.
  • Treatment, partner advice and follow-up depend on the diagnosis.

Frequently asked questions

Does a genital sore always mean an STI?

No. Irritation, trauma, inflammatory skin disease and illness-associated aphthous ulcers are other possibilities. Infections still need to be considered, so assessment is important rather than assuming either cause.

Can a painless sore be important?

Yes. Syphilis often causes a painless sore, and some persistent lesions have other causes needing treatment. Pain level alone cannot establish how serious a lesion is.

Can I tell herpes from syphilis by looking?

Not reliably. Typical patterns overlap and may be absent. A clinician may use a lesion swab, blood tests and the history to establish the cause.

Should I still get checked if the sore has healed?

Yes, particularly if an STI is possible or the problem recurs. A syphilis sore can disappear while infection remains, and a healed lesion may require a different testing or follow-up plan.

Is a genital wart the same as an ulcer?

No. Warts usually form raised growths; an ulcer is an open break in the surface. An irritated or bleeding growth still needs examination rather than a visual assumption.

Can I put hydrocortisone or wart remover on it?

Do not use them on an undiagnosed lesion without advice. Prescribed steroids help certain inflammatory conditions, but ordinary wart-removal acids and inappropriate creams can damage genital skin.

What can help stinging when I urinate?

Gently pouring lukewarm water over the external area while urinating may help. Ask about appropriate pain relief. If you cannot pass urine because of pain, seek urgent care.

Do condoms prevent every infection that causes sores?

They reduce risk but do not cover all potentially affected skin. Avoid sexual contact during an active herpes outbreak and follow the clinic’s infection-specific advice about treatment and resuming sex.

Do genital sores cause infertility?

Not as a general rule. PID from infections such as chlamydia or gonorrhoea can damage the tubes, but that risk should not be assigned to every herpes lesion, wart or skin irritation. The diagnosis determines the relevant risks.

What should I do if I am pregnant?

Contact your maternity or sexual-health team promptly about new sores or possible herpes or syphilis exposure. Assessment and treatment can affect pregnancy and birth planning; do not wait for the lesion to heal on its own.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
